c.v: A link in a robot model has a visual shape, so that it shows up in the Gazebo window. List everything else the link needs before the physics engine can simulate it correctly, and say in one line each what goes wrong without it. Take 10 minutes.

A collision shape, which is what contacts, friction and the ground act on; without it the link falls through the floor and nothing can touch it. A mass in kilograms. An inertia tensor in kg m², about the centre of mass, together with the pose of the centre of mass in the link frame; without them SDF quietly gives the link 1 kg and 1 kg m² on every axis, and URDF gives it nothing, so Gazebo drops the link. A pose, which places the link frame in the model and defines the axes that the inertia, the shapes and the joint axis refer to. A joint to its parent, with a type and an axis in a known frame, because a link without one is a separate free body. Everything in SI units: metres, kilograms, seconds and radians.

You pass if you had the collision shape, the mass, the inertia about the centre of mass and a frame to express them in, with a consequence for each. Missing the frame, the joint or the units is a partial pass. Missing the collision shape or the inertia is a fail.

A link needs more than the shape a camera in the viewer sees: a separate collision shape, what contacts, friction and the ground actually act on; a mass; an inertia tensor about the centre of mass, the rotational equivalent of mass; a pose, fixing the frame every one of those numbers is expressed in; and a joint to a parent, without which it is a separate free body rather than part of the robot. Every number is expected in SI units, metres, kilograms, seconds and radians, and no format checks that.

The problem is that a model can look correct in the viewer while being physically meaningless, because the visual shape a person sees and the numbers physics uses are two separate things nothing forces to agree. A link with a visual shape and nothing else renders perfectly and falls straight through the floor, since there is no collision shape for the ground to act on.

The collision shape and the visual shape have separate jobs: physics only sees collisions, and a camera or a lidar only sees visuals, which is why a detailed visual mesh is normally paired with a plain box or cylinder as its collision. Inertia for a simple shape has a closed formula from its mass and dimensions, and a genuine inertia tensor also satisfies the triangle inequality, no one principal moment larger than the sum of the other two, which a hand-typed value can violate unnoticed until checked.

What goes wrong under pressure is that nothing in the format checks any of this against reality. A mesh authored in millimetres and read as metres produces a building-sized robot that passes every validity check, since a huge box is still a physically legal one. A link with no inertia block is not an error either: one format quietly substitutes a default mass and inertia, the other drops the link and everything below it, and either way the simulation keeps running as if nothing were wrong. A checker catching a broken inertia tensor has no idea what your robot's true masses are; only the datasheet catches a wrong, legal number.

You meet exactly this in the interview question itself: naming everything besides the visual shape a link needs before physics can simulate it correctly, a collision shape, a mass, an inertia about the centre of mass, a frame and a joint, and saying what breaks without each.

subs.title: Geometry, frames, collision, joints, mass, inertia, units

c.v: Here is one wheel of a small differential-drive robot in SDF, the format Gazebo reads:

blocks.text:
<link name="left_wheel">
  <pose>0.07 0.12 0.05 -1.5708 0 0</pose>            <!-- in the model frame: x y z roll pitch yaw -->
  <inertial>
    <mass>0.2</mass>                                   <!-- kg -->
    <inertia>                                          <!-- kg m^2, about the centre of mass -->
      <ixx>0.00014</ixx> <ixy>0</ixy> <ixz>0</ixz>
      <iyy>0.00014</iyy> <iyz>0</iyz> <izz>0.00025</izz>
    </inertia>
  </inertial>
  <collision name="collision">
    <geometry><cylinder><radius>0.05</radius><length>0.03</length></cylinder></geometry>
  </collision>
  <visual name="visual">
    <geometry><cylinder><radius>0.05</radius><length>0.03</length></cylinder></geometry>
  </visual>
</link>
<joint name="left_wheel_joint" type="revolute">
  <parent>chassis</parent>
  <child>left_wheel</child>
  <axis><xyz>0 0 1</xyz></axis>                        <!-- in the joint frame, here the wheel's own frame -->
</joint>

places the child link's frame in the parent link's frame, so the wheel sits at z = −0.03 m from the chassis centre, which is 0.08 m above the ground. The joint frame is the child's frame, and an
left out defaults to (1, 0, 0). URDF describes one robot as a tree of links: it has no world, no closed loops and no nested models, and it carries simulator settings only inside
extension tags. Gazebo converts a URDF to SDF when it loads it. On the way, links joined by
joints are merged into their parent, and a link without an

block, or with a mass of zero, is dropped, together with its joint and everything below it, with warnings that the link "is not modeled in sdf". In a typical ROS setup one xacro file produces the URDF,
spawns the same description into Gazebo.

c.v: The last two lines are the reason to compute rather than guess. A chassis measured in millimetres gets an inertia a million times too large, and it passes every check, because a 300 m box is physical. A mistyped

breaks the triangle inequality, which sdformat does check: it reports that the link "has invalid inertia", and by default Gazebo then refuses to load the world. Real links aren't solid primitives, and a CAD tool gives better numbers for a real part. For a primitive, SDF 1.11, which Gazebo Harmonic reads, can compute the values itself:
takes the link's collision shapes and a
in kg/m³, 1000 by default, and overwrites any mass and inertia you wrote.

The collision shape and the visual shape have separate jobs, and Gazebo uses each in different places. The physics engine sees only collisions: contacts, friction, the ground under the wheels. Cameras and the GPU lidar are rendered, so they see only visuals. A detailed visual mesh with a box or cylinder as its collision is the usual choice, because contact checks between meshes cost far more than between primitives.
Xacro removes the repetition. It is a macro language for XML that the
command expands into plain URDF, with properties, arithmetic in
and macros with parameters. A macro that computes a cylinder's inertia from its size means the numbers can't drift apart from the geometry:

blocks.text:
<xacro:macro name="cylinder_inertial" params="mass radius length">
  <inertial>
    <mass value="${mass}"/>
    <inertia ixx="${mass * (3 * radius * radius + length * length) / 12}" ixy="0" ixz="0"
             iyy="${mass * (3 * radius * radius + length * length) / 12}" iyz="0"
             izz="${mass * radius * radius / 2}"/>
  </inertial>
</xacro:macro>

<xacro:cylinder_inertial mass="0.2" radius="0.05" length="0.03"/>

subs.title: Visual versus collision shapes; zero inertia

c.v: Visual and collision shapes that disagree give the robot's sensors and its body two different worlds. A wall with a visual but no collision shows up in the lidar scan and the camera, and the robot drives through it. A wall with a collision but no visual stops the robot, and the lidar, which is rendered, never sees it. The same holds for the robot itself: a collision box larger than the chassis makes it catch on door frames that its visual clears. To see the collision shapes, right-click a model in the Gazebo window and pick Collisions from its View menu, which also draws the centre of mass, the inertia, the joints and the frames.
Missing or zero inertia fails in three different ways. An SDF link without
silently gets 1 kg and 1 kg m², as in the exercise. A URDF link without it, or with zero mass, disappears in the conversion, with a warning from

block and "is not modeled in sdf", unless a fixed joint merges it into its parent. A link with mass but zero moments passes the SDF check, because zero moments are still positive semi-definite, and then DART warns that the value "should be positive and greater than zero" and that results might not be physically meaningful. The physics shows why. The angular acceleration is torque divided by moment of inertia, so a 0.01 N m contact torque over one 1 ms step changes the wheel's spin by 0.01 × 0.001 / 0.00025 = 0.04 rad/s with the right inertia, and by 10 000 rad/s with a moment of 10⁻⁹ kg m². Tiny moments make links jitter and spin up; zero ones leave the result undefined.

Placeholder values survive in real models, so check the ones you inherit. The Jazzy URDF tutorial gives its 10 kg cylinder of radius 0.2 m and length 0.6 m an inertia of 10⁻³ kg m² on every axis. The formulas give 0.4 kg m² across and 0.2 kg m² about the axis, 400 and 200 times more. The TurtleBot3 Waffle in

, the robot the Test Bench drives, gives each 0.1 kg wheel of radius 0.033 m 0.001 kg m² on every axis, where a solid cylinder has 5.4 × 10⁻⁵ about its axle, about 18 times less. With velocity-controlled wheels and no effort limit, that one hardly changes how the robot drives; it would matter as soon as the wheels were driven by torque.
